highlights.title: How GenAI Adoption Affects Job Demand: Evidence from India
highlights.summary: Using job-postings data from a leading Indian platform and ChatGPT's November 2022 launch as a quasi-natural experiment, the study measures how GenAI adoption shifts labor demand across occupations in a large emerging economy.

highlights.title: Past Automation and Future AI: How Weak Links Tame the Growth Explosion
highlights.summary: Task-based growth accounting shows capital task productivity has grown ~5 percentage points per year faster than labor task productivity in the US economy, quantifying automation's historical displacement of labor tasks and its implications for AI-driven futures.

highlights.title: Who Counts as Exposed? Measurement Choices in an Open, Re-estimable Index of Occupational AI Exposure
highlights.summary: An open task-level occupational AI exposure index shows that design choices around context and calibration can produce widely varying estimates of which workers are exposed, with measurement decisions materially affecting policy-relevant headcounts of at-risk workers.

highlights.title: Indeed Hiring Lab: There is no AI Jobpocalypse, but plenty of AI-nxiety
highlights.summary: Indeed Hiring Lab's 2026 outlook review finds no aggregate 'jobpocalypse' in US posting data while documenting widespread worker anxiety about AI displacement, providing a current qualitative-quantitative snapshot from the largest job-postings database.

highlights.title: AI and the Two Margins of Work: Why Job Losses Show Up Before Job Creation
highlights.summary: Combining historical computing-era firm data with a theoretical model, the paper shows AI-driven job losses are recorded in payroll statistics promptly while compensating job creation by new entrants lags by years; firms entering after 1978 held 42% of employment by the measurement period.

highlights.title: AI-Driven Transformation of Digital Platform Work: A Task-Based Model for Measuring Labour Disruption and Vulnerability, with Early Evidence from Online Freelancing in Kenya
highlights.summary: A task-based disruption model applied to Kenyan online freelance data finds that AI vulnerability varies sharply within occupational categories depending on work arrangement, with early evidence suggesting platform freelancers face higher intra-occupation displacement risk than conventional measures imply.

highlights.title: Productivity Without Prosperity? Who Captures the Economic Gains from Workplace Artificial Intelligence?
highlights.summary: A capture-accounting framework linking published field experiments (14–40% productivity gains on specific tasks) through adoption curves to economy-wide wage effects finds that productivity benefits accrue disproportionately to capital owners and high-skill workers rather than median wage earners.

highlights.title: Jobs and Technology: An Integrated View
highlights.summary: A World Bank Research Observer paper integrating evidence on industrial robots and AI across developing economies identifies two key adoption drivers and estimates heterogeneous displacement effects, with new empirical analysis of diffusion speeds across income groups.

highlights.title: Revelio Labs: Average Earnings Markdowns Fell from ~30% Pre-2022 to ~20% in 2023–2025
highlights.summary: Using linked workforce and wage data, Revelio Labs estimates that employer wage-setting power (monopsony markdown) fell from approximately 30% before 2022 to roughly 20% in 2023–2025, with markdowns remaining highest in the public sector and professional services.

highlights.title: Perceived Differences in Activity and Experience Between Developing Software With and Without AI
highlights.summary: A comparative study of software engineers working with and without generative AI tools documents shifts in task composition and required skill sets, providing early behavioral evidence on how AI is reshaping software engineering roles and career trajectories.

highlights.title: Artificial intelligence diffusion, adaptive Human-Capital Transformation, and unequal development: evidence from a 50-country panel
highlights.summary: A 229-observation, 50-country panel finds that AI capacity, human capital, and institutional quality jointly predict unequal development outcomes, with AI diffusion widening skill-wage gaps in lower-institutional-quality settings.

highlights.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on IT Jobs: Opportunities, Displacement Risks, and Skill Transformation
highlights.summary: A review of AI's impact on IT employment finds evidence of task redistribution, productivity shifts, and changing recruitment expectations, with displacement risks concentrated in routine coding and testing roles and growth in AI-augmentation skill demand.

highlights.title: The Expanding Elite Premium: Task-Biased Technological Change and Higher Education Stratification in China
highlights.summary: Using three waves of the China Household Income Survey (2013–2023), the paper finds that the wage premium for graduates of elite-tier institutions expanded significantly over the period, consistent with task-biased technological change and early GenAI diffusion widening returns to elite credentials.

highlights.title: Artificial Intelligence and Work: Evidence from the Portuguese Labor Market
highlights.summary: A thesis-level empirical study using Portuguese matched employer-employee data examines AI's effects on job replacement and productivity, finding occupation-level displacement evidence differentiated from prior automation waves.

highlights.title: Indeed Hiring Lab: 2026 Q3 US Business-to-Business Labor Market Update
highlights.summary: Indeed's Q3 2026 B2B sector update shows job postings up year-over-year in most B2B categories, providing a current sectoral benchmark for white-collar and professional hiring trends against which AI displacement signals can be calibrated.

themes: No aggregate US jobpocalypse yet, but sector- and task-level displacement signals are diverging sharply from headline job-posting trends
Measurement choices in AI exposure indices materially change which workers are counted as at risk, underscoring need for open, re-estimable methodologies
Productivity gains from GenAI (14–40% in experiments) are not translating uniformly to median wages, with capital and high-skill workers capturing disproportionate share
